client: I just don't feel like doing anything anymore since my dog passed away last month. We used to go on walks every morning, and now when I see other people walking their dogs, I just feel this heavy sadness. Part of me thinks talking about it won't bring him back, so what's the point?
therapist: It sounds like your dog was such an important part of your daily life and routine, and this loss has left a big void. While talking about it won't bring him back, it might help you process the grief and find new ways to honor his memory. What's one small thing you could do today that might help you feel connected to him?

client:
I don't know... everything just feels empty now. Even small things like taking his favorite walk route just makes me cry. Part of me thinks I should just try to forget and move on, but then I feel guilty for even thinking that way. 

I did keep his collar though. It's sitting on my dresser but I can't bring myself to touch it. Looking at it makes my chest hurt so bad. Maybe that's stupid.
therapist: Your feelings aren't stupid at all - they show how deeply you loved your companion. Keeping his collar is a beautiful way to honor that bond, even if it's painful right now. What do you think your dog would want for you during this difficult time?

client: I know he'd want me to be happy, but that just makes me feel worse because I can't seem to move on. Every time I see his collar, I start crying all over again - it's been months and I still feel this overwhelming sadness. Part of me thinks maybe I should just pack his things away so I don't have to face the pain every day.
therapist: Grief doesn't follow a timeline, and it's okay that you're still feeling this deep sadness - it shows how meaningful your bond was. While packing things away might bring temporary relief, I wonder if there might be a middle ground where you could keep just one special item visible? What feels most true to your heart right now?

client: I know you're right about grief not having a timeline, but it's been two years since my mom passed and I still can't even look at her things without breaking down. Keeping something out sounds nice in theory, but every time I see her favorite coffee mug on the shelf, I just feel this crushing guilt that I wasn't there enough at the end. Maybe I'm not ready for any of her things to be out yet.
therapist: It sounds like your grief is still carrying some heavy guilt along with the sadness, and that makes seeing her belongings especially painful. These feelings of "not being there enough" must be so difficult to sit with—what do you think your mom would say about that guilt you're holding?

client:
I don't know what she'd say...that's the worst part. I keep replaying all the times I canceled plans with her because I was "too busy" with work. Now I'll never get to tell her how sorry I am. The guilt just eats at me every time I see her favorite coffee mug still sitting in my cupboard. 

It's hard to imagine her perspective when I'm stuck in all these regrets. Part of me thinks she'd say it's okay, but another part worries she died feeling like I didn't care enough. That thought keeps me up at night.
therapist: It's clear how much you wish you could have those moments back, and that longing speaks to how deeply you did care about her. The fact that this pain persists shows how much your relationship mattered—what might it feel like to write her that apology you wish you could say?

client: I don't know if writing an apology would help—she's gone now, and it just feels too late. Sometimes I think maybe I'm punishing myself by dwelling on this because part of me believes I don't deserve to feel better about it. The guilt keeps coming back no matter what I try.
therapist: It sounds like this guilt has become a way to stay connected to your mom, even though it's painful. What would it feel like to consider that holding onto this pain might actually be keeping you from fully honoring the love you did share?

client:
That's a really hard thought to sit with. Part of me feels like if I let go of the guilt, it would mean I didn't care enough about her. But another part wonders if you're right - maybe this pain is just keeping me stuck. 

It's just... the guilt feels like the last thing connecting me to her. What if I lose that and then there's nothing left? That thought terrifies me more than the guilt does.
therapist: You're describing such an important tension - between wanting to honor your mom's memory and fearing that releasing the guilt might somehow diminish your connection to her. What if there were ways to stay connected to her that didn't require holding onto this pain?

client:
I don't know... the guilt is the only thing that makes me feel close to her now. If I let that go, it's like I'm letting her go all over again. The pain is awful, but at least it's something real we still share. 

What if I stop feeling guilty and then realize I can't remember her voice anymore? That terrifies me more than the sadness.
therapist: It sounds like this guilt has become a sacred space where you keep your mom close, even though it hurts. I wonder if we could explore other ways to honor your connection—ones that might feel more like love than punishment? What's one happy memory of her that still makes you smile when you think of it?

client: I don't know... it feels wrong to focus on happy memories when I should be remembering all the times I let her down. The guilt is what keeps me honest about how I failed her. But... I do remember how she used to make my favorite pancakes every Sunday morning. That memory just makes me feel worse though, because I took those moments for granted.
therapist: It's understandable that happy memories might feel bittersweet right now, but noticing how you "took those moments for granted" shows how much you've grown—would your mom want you to only remember the regrets, or also the love in those Sunday mornings?

client: I know she wouldn't want me to only focus on the regrets, but that's what keeps coming up automatically. The love is there too, but it almost hurts more to remember the good times because they're gone now. I feel guilty that I can't just focus on the positive like everyone seems to expect me to.
therapist: It makes complete sense that the happy memories feel painful too—grief isn't about choosing between love and regret, but learning to hold both. What if we gently explored how those Sunday pancakes might become a way to honor her, rather than just a reminder of loss?
